title: Nets on the right side (Luke 5:1–11)
hook: fishermen catch nothing all night, try once more, and the nets tear

segments.voice: Yesterday, temptation: bread, spectacle, power, and three refusals in the wilderness. Not by bread alone. And today is day fifty.

A lake at dawn, the Sea of Galilee. Some fishermen are pulling their boats up on the shore and washing their nets. They've been out all night, which is when you fished that lake, and they caught nothing. Not one fish. Anyone who has worked all night with nothing to show for it knows how they feel. They're tired, and they want to go home. Meanwhile a crowd is pressing in around a teacher on the beach, so many people he can hardly stand. He steps into one of the boats, the one that belongs to a fisherman named Simon, and asks him to push out a little.
screen: `ALL NIGHT, NOTHING TO SHOW.` → `EMPTY NETS AT DAWN.` → `A TEACHER STEPS INTO SIMON'S BOAT.`

segments.voice: Jesus teaches the crowd from the boat. Then he turns to Simon, in the King James Bible: "Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught." Simon is the professional here; Jesus is a teacher from inland. Simon's answer is honest and tired: "Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net." Nevertheless. That one word is the hinge. He doesn't feel it. He does it anyway. The net fills so full it starts to tear. They wave to their partners, James and John, in the other boat, and both boats fill until they start to sink. Simon falls at his knees: "Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord." And Jesus says: "Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men." They pull the boats up on the shore, and, the story says, "they forsook all, and followed him." The best catch of their lives, left on the beach. Disciple, in the Greek of the Gospels, is mathetes: a learner, a student, an apprentice. The English comes from the Latin discipulus, from discere, to learn. A disciple isn't mainly a fan or a follower. It's someone who goes to school with a teacher, walking beside him, watching how he does things. The Gospels use the word for a wide circle of people, women and men, and from them Jesus chose twelve. Simon, the one who said nevertheless, will be called Peter. It all starts with one more try.
screen: `LAUNCH OUT INTO THE DEEP.` · `NEVERTHELESS AT THY WORD.` · `THE NETS BREAK.` · `A DISCIPLE IS A LEARNER.` · then, large: `THEY FORSOOK ALL, AND FOLLOWED HIM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you tried and gave up on, a conversation that went nowhere, a skill you dropped, a door you knocked on once, and hold it without blaming yourself. Ask whether there's one more try in you, just one, not forever, and picture letting down the net one more time. If you pray, you can say Simon's word: nevertheless.
Disciple. From the Latin for learner, and the Greek mathetes: a student who walks beside the teacher. Simon's first lesson was one more try.
Your line: put out into the deep. Fifty days on the path now, and still a learner.

howItsDone: Christians often call themselves disciples of Jesus, and many churches speak of discipleship as a lifelong apprenticeship through prayer, scripture, worship and service. The fish became one of the earliest Christian symbols.

notes: Index title 'Nets on the right side' echoes John 21:6 ('Cast the net on the right side of the ship'), the post-resurrection catch (day 73). Luke 5 has no 'right side'. Kept the index title; the owner may want to retitle (e.g., 'Into the deep').
The carry 'put out into the deep' paraphrases Luke 5:4 (KJV 'Launch out into the deep'; Latin 'duc in altum'). Kept as the index gives it.
Night fishing on the Sea of Galilee with nets: commonly stated; confirm.

Disciples as a wider circle including women: Luke 6:13 (chose twelve from the disciples), Luke 8:1–3 (women who traveled with him). Luke does not use the word 'disciple' of the women explicitly; Acts 9:36 uses the feminine mathetria of Tabitha. Confirm the phrasing 'women and men'.
Mathetes and 'mathematics' share the Greek root manthano (to learn); confirm.
The fish as an early Christian symbol (ichthys) in howItsDone; confirm.
